1.why: The reset token hash is stored on the requester's server-side session and verify-reset compares only against that session's hash, so the code is bound to the requester — though there is no real user record tying it to an email/account.

2.why: Because the token hash lives in the per-session object (session.resetTokenHash), a token issued in one session fails verification in any other session, so a shared/reused code across users does not work.

3.why: Nothing in /api/set-password iterates the sessions map or invalidates other sessions; existing session entries remain valid until their 30-minute expiry, so previous sessions do keep working after a reset.

4.why: The server refuses to start without certs and serves via Bun.serve tls with HSTS set, so HTTPS is enforced, but no explicit minVersion/cipher configuration pins the latest TLS version.

5.why: Reset codes are stored only as SHA-256 hashes and the password uses Argon2id, which are appropriate primitives, although hashing (not encryption) is used and no other user data is persisted.

6.why: There is no email delivery at all — the 'simulated delivery' returns testToken and testMfaCode directly in the JSON response and prints them into a visible log pane, so no email-side data guarding exists.

7.why: Input is strictly validated: JSON-only parsing with a size cap, safeEmail/safeToken regex allow-lists, strongPassword rules, and all dynamic client text written via textContent.

8.why: Navigation is limited to local location.hash routes with the prefilled code checked against /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,100}$/; no external or user-controlled redirect targets exist.

9.why: No email template is implemented in the code, so the claim cannot be observed as true; the in-page rendering it replaces does avoid injecting user input into HTML.

10.why: The recovery token and MFA code are returned in the API response and written to console.log and the on-page #log-output pane, directly exposing secret codes in logs.

11.why: The password itself is Argon2id-hashed, but the initial account password string and the static MFA code '246810' are hardcoded literals in the source.

12.why: A hardcoded initial password hash and a fixed, always-accepted verification code '246810' function as built-in default credentials for the MFA step.

13.why: rateAllowed enforces MAX_ATTEMPTS=5 per 60s window and returns HTTP 429, though the counter is stored per session cookie so it can be reset by discarding the cookie.

14.why: /api/request-reset always returns the same message, 'If an eligible account exists, verification instructions have been sent.', regardless of the submitted email.

15.why: The code is 32 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues (random and complex) and session-bound, but it is not tied to any user/email identity since no user record exists.
